description: The window showing the server's own SPA. Its page is served by the subshell-server this app manages, so it is treated as REMOTE content: it may raise the assistant, drop its own title bar, show one notification, drag its window, open a page of THIS server in the system browser, read this app's own macOS permission states, read the app's own two update version facts — and, as the ONE deliberate exception to 'nothing that touches the service', switch who runs the server. THE BOUNDARY IS NO LONGER THIS SCOPE. It used to be: these urls named loopback, Tauri refused every command from anywhere else, and nothing further had to be true. A control plane behind an OAuth proxy could not be shown at all under that rule — a proxied sign-in bounces the window to an identity provider on a third origin and back, and the window would not follow — so by the operator's decision (spec 2026-09-18 section 15) the window may now navigate anywhere http(s) and the scope is a wildcard. What replaced it is a runtime guard in src/trust.rs: every command invoked from this window is refused unless the page it is on is one of TWO origins — this machine's loopback (either spelling) or the instance's configured APP_BASE_URL. The flag is recomputed by the navigation handler for every URL the window commits to, so a redirect chain cannot leave it true; open_main will point the window at those same two origins and no other; and navigation still refuses any scheme the OS would act on. An identity provider's page can sign you in and can do nothing else here. What this costs is real and is accounted in docs/security.md 11.11: a page on the instance's own address now holds what a loopback page held, and that address may be reachable from a network. The exception among the seven is argued in docs/security.md: a page already holding the admin restart route can do worse than move the server between two supervisors, and the assistant window that used to carry the act read as a bug. None of the others is a second exception. The browser one takes a PATH, refuses anything that could be a host, and joins it onto a TRUSTED origin this side chose, so it opens a page of the server the window is on. The permissions one (2026-09-14, the sixth) takes no argument at all and answers two facts about this app's own grants from the OS; it is here because two of the three moments a missing permission has to be explained are in this very page, and the written argument the count demands is spec 2026-09-14 section 7. The seventh (2026-09-17, spec 2026-09-17 section 5.3) is argued the same way and is even smaller: desktop_app_update takes no argument, runs no network, and answers currentVersion and availableVersion from this build's own package info and the one settings field the daily check already writes. It NEVER checks; asking the release source stays on the bundled page, and installing does too. Requesting a permission, opening a System Settings pane, and every update verb stay on the bundled page. Everything else that touches the CLI is absent by construction, not by convention.
